shots.text: Triangular eyes, the pupils pierced right through.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.text: Above them, an elaborate hairstyle, worked in fired clay.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.text: The style is called Nok, after a culture of central Nigeria.
shots.desc: wooded plateau of central Nigeria at first light, granite outcrops, mist in valleys

shots.text: Its excavators describe Nok as the earliest large-scale sculptural tradition in sub-Saharan Africa.
shots.desc: excavation trench edge at dawn, trowel and brush on red earth

shots.text: Yet they found no evidence of a state, of towns, or of an elite.
shots.desc: open savanna woodland, no buildings, long shadows

shots.text: So could small, scattered farming communities have made art on this scale?
shots.desc: a lone thatched homestead far off across a millet field at dusk

shots.text: The first of these terracottas was noticed in 1928, during tin mining at the village of Nok.
The British archaeologist Bernard Fagg collected the finds, and gave them a name: the Nok culture.
shots.desc: generic mid-century archive shelves with closed boxes, soft window light, no desk, no person, no papers with writing

shots.text: Many of his pieces came from tin-mine gravels, moved from where they had first lain.
shots.desc: wet alluvial gravels in an old tin-mine cutting, overcast

shots.text: A separate find came in 1943.
shots.desc: road through farmland, 1940s, heat haze

shots.text: According to Fagg's later account, as retold in Archaeology magazine, a terracotta head had been used on a scarecrow in a yam field.
shots.desc: yam mounds in a field, a scarecrow silhouette against sky, head not shown

shots.text: It was brought to him in Jos.
shots.desc: 1940s town street on a plateau, late afternoon, no faces

shots.text: It is known as the Jemaa head, after the village where it was found.
shots.desc: rural village edge, granite boulders, evening smoke

shots.text: In the wake of Fagg's publications, Nok pieces flooded the international art market.
shots.desc: wooden crates stacked in a dim warehouse, straw packing

shots.text: Sites were dug out for sale, and the record of where things lay was lost.
shots.desc: freshly dug pits in red earth at night, torchlight, no people

shots.text: Later, archaeologists from Goethe University Frankfurt went looking.
shots.desc: 4x4 on a dirt track through the plateau, dust

shots.text: All of the team's first thirty sites had been looted.
shots.desc: field of abandoned looters' pits, spoil heaps, grass regrowing

shots.text: In their key study area, plundered sites dominate.
shots.desc: aerial view of pitted ground among farmland

shots.text: Forgeries became a known problem too.
shots.desc: kiln fire in darkness, sparks

shots.text: Today, Nok terracottas are on the International Council of Museums' Red List of objects at risk.
shots.desc: empty museum plinth under a spotlight

shots.text: Very few Nok figures come from recorded excavations, and complete ones are extremely rare.
shots.desc: a single clay fragment on a sieve, soil falling through

shots.text: That loss makes even a simple question hard. When?
shots.desc: soil section with charcoal lenses, side light

shots.text: Britannica still describes Nok as existing between about 500 BCE and 200 CE.
That range came from a handful of early radiocarbon and thermoluminescence dates.
shots.desc: old laboratory bench, glassware, sample tins

shots.text: Museum records vary too: the Cleveland Museum of Art gives this head a thermoluminescence date of 20 to 620 CE.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Cleveland Museum of Art (1995.21) · CC0

shots.text: The Frankfurt team began fieldwork in 2005, and from 2009 its long-term project was funded by the German Research Foundation.
shots.desc: grid of excavation squares, string lines, morning

shots.text: They excavated, built a pottery sequence, and gathered more than two hundred radiocarbon dates.
shots.desc: rows of labelled potsherds on a tarpaulin

shots.text: On their chronology, Nok began around 1500 BC.
Its main phase ran from the ninth to the fourth century BC, when terracottas and iron appear.
And it ended around the turn of the Common Era.
The earliest furnace dates fall somewhere between 800 and 400 BC.
shots.desc: glowing clay furnace mouth at night, charcoal

shots.text: But iron smelting by about 800 BC cannot yet be confirmed.
So who made the figures?
shots.desc: hands pressing wet clay, close up, no face

shots.text: Art this accomplished, the thinking went, must have come from a complex society, with specialists to make it.
shots.desc: lamp-lit museum storeroom, shelves of covered objects

shots.text: Peter Breunig has said that, at first, his team assumed the same.
shots.desc: field notebook open on a trench edge, pencil, wind

shots.text: What they found was smaller.
shots.desc: small clearing seen from above, woodland around

shots.text: Many sites cover roughly one or two hectares.
shots.desc: low hillside with a few hut circles marked out in earth

shots.text: They look like brief occupations, scattered across the land.
shots.desc: wide plateau, a few distant smoke columns far apart

shots.text: No towns, no monuments and no central workshops have been found so far.
shots.desc: empty grassland at noon, heat shimmer

shots.text: Charred grains show what people grew: pearl millet, alongside cowpeas.
shots.credit: Excavation at the Nok site of Ido (cropped) · Louis Champion et al. 2022 · CC BY 4.0

shots.text: Even the iron fits that picture: furnaces seem to have been used only once.
shots.desc: broken clay furnace wall in a trench, slag

shots.text: The team reads that as a sign of travelling specialists, not a central workshop.
shots.desc: footpath winding over hills at dawn

shots.text: As for iron objects, Breunig says everything they recovered fits into one hand.
shots.desc: an open palm dusted with red earth, empty

shots.text: And the sculptures themselves turn up broken.
shots.desc: terracotta-coloured sherds in a pit, unidentifiable shapes

shots.text: Fragments lie in pits, and, as Breunig puts it, the pieces didn't fit together.
shots.desc: a trowel beside scattered fired-clay fragments

shots.text: The team suspects the figures were broken deliberately before burial.
shots.desc: pit cut in section, layers of soil, low sun

shots.text: Gabriele Franke says they can't prove it, but the pattern is striking.
shots.desc: rain beginning on an excavation tarpaulin

shots.text: At Pangwari, excavated between 2011 and 2014, they found a terracotta deposit in a secure archaeological context for the first time.
shots.desc: generic close-up of a trowel cleaning red soil, no finds visible

shots.text: The team interprets some deposits as graves, marked by upright stones in a row; no human remains survive.
shots.desc: a row of plain upright field stones in grassland at dusk, no finds, no people

shots.text: So what kind of society was this?
shots.desc: dusk over a dispersed farming landscape

shots.text: Breunig and Rupp concluded that Nok developed complexity only in terms of ritual.
shots.desc: a row of upright stones at night, low firelight

shots.text: They describe small groups of farmers, living autonomously in dispersed settlements.
shots.desc: a few homesteads spaced far apart across fields, morning

shots.text: The excavators found no evidence of a state or an elite.
shots.desc: open hilltop, no structures, wind in grass

shots.text: That is not proof of absence: they stress that preservation is poor, and the data come from a limited area.
shots.desc: acidic red soil, roots, a single sherd

shots.text: There might have been rulers or chiefs, they write, who left no status markers.
shots.desc: footprints fading on a dirt track

shots.text: But on the evidence so far, Breunig says, highly accomplished art does not necessarily require a complex society.
shots.credit: Nok kneeling figure · Honolulu Museum of Art (8348.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.text: The work is unfinished.
shots.desc: overgrown trench, weeds, collapsed string lines

shots.text: Fieldwork stopped after a deadly attack in 2017; the team has not gone back to the excavation area.
shots.desc: an empty field camp at dusk, folded chairs

shots.text: Why Nok ended is still unknown; the team suggests environmental change as one possibility.
shots.desc: storm light moving across the plateau

shots.text: Gabriele Franke puts it this way.
shots.desc: plateau at last light (NOK05 not obtainable: Wikimedia returned HTTP 429 throughout the build)

shots.text: "The 'mystery of the Nok culture' hasn't been solved – but today we have a much clearer understanding of what that mystery actually is."
shots.credit: Nok seated figure · Louvre (70.1998.11.1) · Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen, Public domain

shots.text: Great art – and, so far, no evidence of a great state.
shots.credit: Nok terracotta head · Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0
